**Case Vignette: Mr. T.**

Mr. T. is a 76-year-old man, slight of build, with a quiet, deliberate way of moving. He has been a warehouse worker for a large distribution center for the past twelve years, a job he took after retiring from a smaller factory. He lives alone in a studio apartment. He came to therapy at the urging of his primary care doctor, who noted his blood pressure was chronically elevated and he had lost weight. Mr. T. agreed to come, but he rarely makes eye contact and speaks in a low, even tone, his hands folded in his lap.

The story he tells is one of a life bisected. Before, there was a village. He was a young man, the eldest son, helping his father with their small rice paddy. He remembers the smell of wet earth, the weight of a full basket on his shoulder, the laughter of his younger siblings. Then the war came. He does not say which war. He says, “The soldiers came. Not our soldiers. Not their soldiers. Just soldiers.” He was not a fighter. He was a civilian, a boy trying to keep his family alive.

The event he returns to, in the quiet of the therapy room, is a single afternoon. He was sent to a neighboring village to trade a few chickens for medicine for his mother, who was sick with fever. He was walking a dirt path through a bamboo grove when the sky opened up with the sound of jets. He dove into a ditch, the mud cold against his chest. He lay there, face down, for what felt like hours, as the ground shook and the air filled with a high, whistling scream that ended in a percussive boom. He remembers the taste of dirt and blood in his mouth from biting his cheek. He remembers a strange, acrid smell. And he remembers, most vividly, the silence that followed. A silence so deep and complete, he thought he had gone deaf. He lay there until dusk, too terrified to move, waiting to be found, or killed.

He eventually made his way back to his village. It was gone. The bamboo grove, the path, the houses, the laughter. All of it. Just a crater and the smell of smoke. He never found his family. He never learned what happened to them.

After that, Mr. T. walked for weeks. He walked south, towards a coast he had only heard of in stories. He survived on roots and rainwater. He does not speak of this part of the journey. He only says, “I kept walking.”

He eventually made it to a refugee camp, then to a sponsor in a new country. He found work. He learned enough English to get by. He built a life, of sorts. But the life, he says, is a shell. Inside the shell, he is still in that ditch.

In the warehouse, Mr. T. is known as a reliable, solitary worker. He prefers the night shift, when the building is mostly empty. He is meticulous about stacking boxes, finding a deep satisfaction in creating neat, stable towers. But the job is a minefield. The sudden roar of a forklift engine makes him drop whatever he is holding. The hydraulic hiss of a loading dock door sends a jolt through his spine that he cannot control. He has learned to anticipate these sounds, bracing himself, counting the seconds until they stop. He has never told a supervisor. He just says he is “jumpy.”

At home, his life is one of ritual. He eats the same meal every night: rice and a single boiled egg. He watches the news with the volume off, reading the captions. He sleeps in a small, windowless alcove he has created in his closet, with a single mattress on the floor. He says it feels “safe.” He does not own a television remote, only a radio, which he keeps tuned to static, a low, white noise that fills the silence he still dreads. He has no friends. He has never had a romantic relationship. He says, “I am not good for people. I have a bad spirit.”

He does not have nightmares in the traditional sense. Instead, he has a recurring feeling. Several times a week, he will wake at 3:00 AM with a certainty that he is back in the ditch, the weight of the mud on his chest, the taste of dirt in his mouth. He will lie perfectly still, barely breathing, for an hour or more, until the feeling passes. He does not scream or thrash. He just waits.

When asked what he hopes to get from therapy, Mr. T. is quiet for a long time. Finally, he says, “I am tired of waiting.” He does not elaborate. He just looks down at his hands, which are still folded, perfectly still, in his lap.
